paper_title: LowRAM: Low-Rank Keys and Amortised Values for Composable KV Cache Compression at Test-Time

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Autoregressive decoding relies on the KV cache, whose memory footprint grows linearly with context length and caps batch size and throughput. Existing post-training methods exploit redundancy across tokens, layers, and feature dimensions, or lower numerical precision. We identify a complementary axis: within each attention head, values are largely predictable from their corresponding keys. We exploit this with value cache amortisation, which fits a lightweight per-head predictor at test time and stores residuals only for the tokens it reconstructs worst, giving $4\times$ near-lossless value compression. The predictor can be initialised by meta-learning for substantially reduced prefill overhead, or fitted from scratch in settings that allow a one-off cost, such as multi-query inference. We pair value amortisation with cross-layer low-rank key compression to produce LowRAM, an asymmetric compression pipeline that stays close to lossless across three model families. By reconstructing only a selected subset of KV pairs at each decoding step, LowRAM can keep decoding overhead minimal and achieve up to $5\times$ higher peak decode throughput at $4\times$ compression. LowRAM further composes with quantisation and eviction, reaching $26.9\times$ compression at $94.5\%$ of baseline performance on long contexts. These results show that treating keys and values as structurally distinct enables efficient, aggressive, and composable KV cache compression.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: Transformers (Vaswani et al., 2017) have become the dominant architecture for language modelling, but their deployment at long context lengths is fundamentally constrained by the compute cost of autoregressive decoding. Modern inference stacks address this via KV cache: the key and value projections of each preceding token are computed once and reused at every subsequent decoding step. This turns decoding from quadratic to linear operation in sequence length, but shifts the bottleneck from compute to memory: the cache grows linearly with context length and batch size, and at long contexts comes to dominate the models activation footprint. wide range of architectural responses to this bottleneck have been proposed, including linear attention and state-space alternatives that replace the cache with fixed-size recurrent hidden state (Katharopoulos et al., 2020; Gu & Dao, 2023; Dao & Gu, 2024), and sparse, sliding-window, grouped-query, and multi-head latent attention variants that reduce per-token cache size architecturally (Ainslie et al., 2023; DeepSeek-AI et al., 2024). However, these approaches require pretraining or substantial finetuning, and most open-weight models still rely on grouped-query attention with full KV cache (Grattafiori et al., 2024; Jiang et al., 2023; Team et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2025a). This has motivated parallel line of post-training KV cache compression methods operating on frozen pretrained models. Existing methods fall into three families: eviction, which discards unimportant entries (Xiao et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2023; Li et al., 2024; Cai et al., 2025); quantisation, which lowers Equal contribution.

See Appendix for description of how compression is computed. the precision of stored entries (Liu et al., 2024; Hooper et al., 2024; Dong et al., 2024); and low-rank decomposition, which approximates KV matrices with smaller, factorised representations (Yu et al., 2024; Chang et al., 2025; Saxena et al., 2024). These families are largely orthogonal, exploiting redundancies along different axes of the cache. This leaves the redundancy between keys and values largely unexplored. Keys and values are computed from the same representation, and although they serve different functions, their shared origin induces predictable relationship between them. We exploit this redundancy by using the keys as source from which the value cache can be recovered. We first compare several predictive relationships within and across layers under matched memory budget and find that reconstructing current-layer values from current-layer keys best preserves downstream performance. Based on this finding, we introduce value cache amortisation: during prefill, we fit lightweight per-head network to map cached keys to their associated values. We then rank tokens by reconstruction error and store residual corrections only for the least accurately predicted values. The resulting value cache consists of the network parameters and sparse set of residuals. During decoding, values are recovered by applying the network to the keys and adding the stored corrections, as illustrated in Figure 2. Amortising the values still requires keys to be retained, both for attention and as inputs to the learned map. complete compression scheme must therefore reduce the key cache as well. Our source-target analysis suggests that applying the same predictive strategy to the keys leads to less downstream performance than for values. Instead, for keys, prior work points to low-rank decomposition: their energy is concentrated in relatively small number of feature directions, producing short spectral tail and correspondingly small approximation error at reduced rank (Saxena et al., 2024). These findings motivate an asymmetric design: values are reconstructed from keys, while the keys themselves are compressed according to their low-rank structure. LowRAM realises this design by pairing value cache amortisation with xKV (Chang et al., 2026), which shares low-rank basis across layers within each group to exploit alignment between their dominant key-cache subspaces. Contributions. We identify within-head key-to-value predictability as previously underexplored source of KV-cache redundancy. Building on this observation, we introduce value cache amortisation, which replaces most stored values with context-adapted predictor and retains residuals only for the hardest-to-predict tokens. We propose LowRAM, an asymmetric pipeline that combines amortised values with crosslayer low-rank key compression. LowRAM remains close to lossless at moderate compression across three model families and composes with quantisation and eviction, reaching 26.9 compression while retaining 94.5% of baseline performance.

sections.title: 2 RELATED WORKS
sections.content: Low-Rank Decomposition of KVs. Training-free SVD-based KV compression largely targets per-layer redundancy, via activation-aware or grouped SVD on the KV projection weights (Yuan et al., 2025; Yu et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2024; Chang et al., 2025; Yan et al., 2025), projecting attention into an offline-fitted eigen-subspace (Saxena et al., 2024), or direct channel pruning (Xu et al., 2025). Complementary learned-projection methods (Lin et al., 2025; Shi et al., 2025; Benfenati et al., 2026; Hao et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026; Lesens et al., 2025; Zhu et al., 2025; Shaikh et al., 2026) reach similar ratios with trained or online-adapted projectors. xKV (Chang et al., 2026) instead exploits cross-layer redundancy, sharing single SVD basis across contiguous layer groups since adjacent layers share dominant singular vectors. Eviction. Eviction reduces KV cache memory by discarding unimportant tokens. Early methods keep attention sinks and recent window (Xiao et al., 2024), or mix of recent and high-attention tokens (Zhang et al., 2023). Later work selects tokens using an observation window (Li et al., 2024), or allocates budgets per layer (Cai et al., 2025) or per head (Ge et al., 2024; Feng et al., 2025; Tang et al., 2025). Query-agnostic methods instead score tokens by how well they support reconstructing the context (Kim et al., 2025; Jegou & Jeblick, 2026). Quantisation. Quantisation compresses the KV cache by lowering the precision of stored keys and values. However, these exhibit channel-wise outliers (Dettmers et al., 2022; Xiao et al., 2023) that dominate uniform quantisation grid, so naive quantisation degrades sharply below 4 bits (Liu et al., 2024; Hooper et al., 2024). Sub-4-bit methods therefore target these outliers by quantising keys channel-wise and values token-wise (Liu et al., 2024), allocating bit-widths per token (Yang et al., 2024a; He et al., 2024; Dong et al., 2024) or per layer (Li et al., 2025), inverting positional embeddings before quantisation (Hooper et al., 2024), or removing outliers with random rotations (Ashkboos et al., 2024; Han et al., 2026; Zandieh et al., 2026). AQUA-KV (Shutova et al., 2025) instead quantises prediction residual, using linear adapters that exploit both inter-layer and intra-layer dependencies: keys are predicted from previous-layer keys, while values are predicted jointly from previous-layer values and current-layer keys. Our amortised value cache uses context-adapted prediction of values from keys within each attention head, storing residuals only for tokens that are hard to reconstruct.

For values, we introduce amortisation, learned associative memory that predicts each tokens value vector directly from its key, fit once per context, and retains residuals only for the values the predictor reconstructs poorly. Prior to both decomposition and prediction, we invert RoPE, following evidence that pre-RoPE representations are more amenable to compression (Hooper et al., 2024; Su et al., 2025; Sun et al., 2025a), with the rotation reapplied at attention time. Both predictor fitting and value reconstruction use the pre-RoPE keys reconstructed by xKV. During decoding, generated key-values are stored exactly in the cache. 3.1 IDENTIFYING THE PREDICTIVE STRUCTURE OF THE KV CACHE Prior work has explored predictive compression of the KV cache using inter-layer and intra-layer dependencies (Shutova et al., 2025) or across tokens (Hao et al., 2026).Here, we focus on learning mapping from keys to values within individual attention heads. To determine which representation is best suited to predictive compression within our framework, we perform source-target analysis over the KV cache. For each layer, we train the same predictor to reconstruct either the current-layer keys or values while varying the available source representation. Specifically, we consider previous-layer keys (KL1), previous-layer values (VL1), their concatenation (KVL1), current-layer values (VL), and current-layer keys (KL). To match our proposed compression scheme, each predictor is paired with residual store, with the residual budget fixed across all configurations. All configurations are evaluated under the same 3 compression budget using both reconstruction error and recovered LongBench performance. Figure 3 shows that reconstructing values from current-layer keys, KL VL, achieves the highest recovered downstream performance among the configurations evaluated. This source-target pair therefore forms the basis of our proposed method. Our comparison revisits the probing configurations examined by AQUA-KV (Shutova et al., 2025) (Figure 2), evaluating them within our predictor and residual-storage framework using both reconstruction error and recovered LongBench performance. Under this setting, lower reconstruction error does not necessarily imply better preserved downstream performance. Two further observations are worth noting. First, value reconstruction generally recovers more downstream performance than key reconstruction. Second, reconstruction error correlates only weakly with downstream performance: sourcetarget pairs with similar reconstruction errors can exhibit significantly different recovered performance, and the differing scales of keys and values make their absolute error difficult to compare directly. We therefore base our design decisions primarily on recovered downstream performance rather than reconstruction error.

Selective reconstruction. Reconstructing the complete cache at every decoding step can offset the computational benefit of compression. Following landmark-guided retrieval (Sun et al., 2025a), we partition the prefix into chunks represented by mean-key landmarks, retain outlier chunks and local window exactly, and reconstruct only the top-k chunks selected by the current query. persistent buffer reuses chunks selected across consecutive decoding steps. We additionally replace the exact key cache SVD with randomised Cholesky-QR decomposition, giving 4 speedup with no loss in downstream quality (Chang et al., 2026). Appendix describes the retrieval configuration, kernels, and memory accounting.

sections.title: 4.1 EXPERIMENTAL SETUP
sections.content: Benchmarks. We evaluate on RULER (Hsieh et al., 2024) and LongBench (Bai et al., 2024), and additionally report LongBench filtered to sequences of at least 10K tokens. For this subset we exclude tasks with fewer than 20 samples meeting the length requirement. Appendix gives per-task statistics. All results are reported as recovered performance relative to the uncompressed baseline. We evaluate across three model families: Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3 (Jiang et al., 2023), Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (Grattafiori et al., 2024), and Qwen3.5-4B (Qwen Team, 2026). Qwen3.5-4B is hybrid architecture that interleaves full attention with linear attention layers; only the full attention layers maintain conventional KV cache, so LowRAM is applied to that subset of layers alone, and the compression ratios we report for Qwen3.5-4B are relative to that subsets cache rather than the whole models. Eviction. When combined with LowRAM, we apply eviction before fitting the map, discarding tokens unlikely to be attended to so the MLP need only reconstruct and store residuals for the tokens it retains. Importance is estimated with small CNN predictor adapted from Yang et al. (2025b): during prefill, pre-hook on each attention layer scores every token by predicted future attention (averaged across heads), and we retain the top-ρT positions by this score, with attention sinks (first 8 tokens) and local window (last 64 tokens) kept unconditionally. Quantisation. We quantise with TurboQuant (Zandieh et al., 2026), omitting the 1-bit QJL (Zandieh et al., 2025) error-correction step. Although QJL debiases the inner product estimations, we found that its variance is amplified by Softmax, thus degrading both attention quality and downstream accuracy. For the key cache, xKV factorises the layer-grouped cache as Kl ABl, where holds the shared low-rank basis and Bl is layer-specific; since only scales with context length , we quantise only A, which captures most of the memory reduction (Appendix gives the crossover analysis for when quantising Bl too becomes worthwhile). We use asymmetric precision, 4-bit for the key factor and 2-bit for value residuals. 4.2 END-TO-END COMPRESSION LowRAM retains near-baseline performance at moderate compression across all three model families  (Table 1)  . Mistral-7B and Llama-3.1-8B retain 97.9-99.4% of baseline performance at 3 compression. At 4, recovery remains 96.0-99.6% except for Llama-3.1-8B on RULER, where it falls to 93.9%. We attribute the performance drop at this compression ratio to the reduced residual budget. sections.title: 5 DISCUSSION
sections.content: Our results suggest that keys and values should be compressed differently. Within each attention head, values are largely predictable from their keys. small per-head predictor fitted to the context, with exact residuals kept for the tokens it reconstructs worst, stays close to lossless at 4 value compression and holds up better on LongBench than low-rank compression of the same cache  (Table 5)  . Pairing it with low-rank keys gives LowRAM, which remains close to baseline at moderate compression and combines with quantisation and eviction to reach 26.9 on long contexts. The ablations suggest why prediction suits values. The key-to-value map appears strongly headspecific (sharing one predictor across layers heads costs almost 20 points, Table 7). Keys are harder to predict, and their errors are likely more harmful: key error perturbs the attention logits and can shift attention onto the wrong tokens, whereas value error enters only after the attention weights are fixed. This matches findings on asymmetric KV quantisation (Tao et al., 2025) and may explain why reconstruction error tracks downstream performance so poorly (Figure 3). Residual placement also matters: at fixed budget, error-ranked selection recovers almost all accuracy, whereas random selection loses most of it (Figure 5). LowRAM is best suited to long contexts. The predictors parameters are fixed cost that is only amortised after few thousand tokens (Figure 8). This is why LowRAM degrades more on 4K RULER than on LongBench, and why it combines less cleanly with eviction, which shortens the sequence but leaves this cost unchanged. The choice of initialisation adds second trade-off. Metalearning brings prefill close to baseline speed at small cost in accuracy, while full per-context fitting

sections.title: 6 LIMITATIONS AND FUTURE WORK
sections.content: We have not evaluated long generations, which would require periodically compressing the suffix of newly generated tokens (e.g. every tokens) rather than relying on single prefill-time fit. It is also unclear how much of the learned parametrisation persists across contexts: gains from warm-starting and Slim Attention initialisation suggest part of the key-to-value relationship is shared, while gains from test-time adaptation indicate remaining context-specific component. Understanding this split, and whether hard-to-predict tokens are stable across contexts, could enable more efficient allocation of memory and computation. AI Use Statement. We used generative AI to edit text we had written ourselves and to write and edit code, all of which we reviewed and verified before use. We take responsibility for the final content of this work. Reproducibility Statement. Reproduction settings are in the appendix: value-reconstruction network (B), eviction/quantisation (4.1), meta-learning (E), selective reconstruction (F), benchmarks (G).

sections.title: A EXTENDED RELATED WORKS
sections.content: A.1 TEST-TIME ADAPTATION AND LEARNED ASSOCIATIVE MEMORY separate line of work reframes sequence modelling itself as online learning at inference. The motivating observation is that the distribution of sequences encountered at test time differs substantially from the training distribution, and that model which can fit itself to the stream it is currently processing should enjoy better in-context performance. Test-time training (Sun et al., 2020) gives this idea concrete architectural form. Rather than maintaining fixed memory state, Sun et al. (2025b) treat the state itself as the parameters of small predictive model, updated during inference by self-supervised reconstruction loss over the incoming tokens. This makes the memory sequence-specific map learned online, rather than hand-specified accumulation rule or static summary of the past. Titans (Behrouz et al., 2025) similarly add neural long-term memory trained at test time, using surprise-based gradient update and adaptive forgetting mechanism, and combine it with short-window attention for longer-range storage. This view has roots in Fast Weight Programmers (Schmidhuber, 1992; 1993), where slow controller network writes key-value associations into fast weights. Schlag et al. (2021) later showed that linear attention (Katharopoulos et al., 2020) can be interpreted as such fast-weight memory, with later variants improving the write rule using delta-style corrections and gates (Yang et al., 2024b;c; 2025c). We inherit the core abstraction of this line (a map from keys to values trained by reconstruction loss) but not its deployment regime: the map is fit once, after prefill, to the completed KV cache of pretrained Transformer, and neither the base model nor the attention computation is modified at inference.

sections.title: F SELECTIVE RECONSTRUCTION
sections.content: To reduce decode-time compute, we adopt landmark-guided selective reconstruction, following ShadowKV (Sun et al., 2025a): rather than reconstructing the full key/value cache at every decode step, we retrieve and reconstruct only query-dependent subset of tokens, using inexpensive per-chunk landmarks as cheap proxy for full attention when deciding which tokens to retrieve. Prefill: landmark construction and exact retention. During prefill, keys are partitioned into fixed-size chunks of tokens, and landmark is computed for each chunk as the mean of its keys. Two subsets of chunks are then set aside and kept exact (both keys and values, uncompressed) rather than represented by their landmark: the chunks whose keys are least similar to their own landmark (outlier chunks, as in ShadowKV), and the chunks overlapping the most recent tokens (a local window; unlike the landmark and outlier mechanism, this is not part of ShadowKVs original design). The remaining chunks form the landmark pool used for query-time retrieval at decode time. This exact retention is not free: the landmarks, their chunk indices, and the outlier/local exact keys and values are all additional persistent state on top of the compressed key cache itself. Rather than reporting compression ratio that ignores this, we account for it directly in rank selection. Because xKV shares one low-rank factor across every layer in group rather than factorising each layer independently, this overhead is measured per layer but spent per group: at the point groups decomposition is triggered, we sum the selective-reconstruction overhead of every layer in the group and subtract it from the byte budget implied by the groups target compression ratio before choosing

Landmarks are computed per key/value head, so under grouped-query attention we pool scores across each group of query heads sharing head by taking the max, before selecting chunks. At each decode step, the incoming query is scored against every landmark in the pool, and the top-k chunks (a chunk budget k, equal to the token budget in Table 14 divided by chunk size c) are retrieved and expanded back into token positions. The retrieved positions are combined with the exact outlier and local positions; keys and values, though compressed independently, are reconstructed at this shared set of positions. Persistent reconstruction cache. Following ShadowKV, we avoid redundant reconstruction work across decode steps by keeping persistent buffer of the most recently reconstructed chunks (capacity tokens). At each step, the newly selected chunk set is diffed against what the buffer already holds: chunks selected again are reused as-is, and only chunks newly entering the selection are reconstructed and written into the buffer. This is implemented via fused CUDA kernels adapted from ShadowKV/xKV.
